To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a vaccine can activate lung macrophages to protect mice from lethal bacterial pneumonia in spite of chemotherapy-induced depletion of neutrophils and bone marrow monocytes.
vaccination induces a population of resident macrophages that are protected from chemotherapy and can protect neutropenic mice against a lethal pneumonia.
vaccine-induced lung resident macrophage activation protects mice from bacterial pneumonia during bone marrow-suppressive cytotoxic chemotherapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new vaccines to protect patients with low blood counts from infections during chemotherapy.
the development of novel approaches to prevent life-threatening bacterial pneumonia in cancer patients undergoing bone marrow-depleting chemotherapy.
the role of macrophage heterogeneity in host defense against bacterial pneumonia during chemotherapy-induced neutropenic states.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the authors have identified a new population of macrophages in mouse lungs.
the authors show that lung macrophages are the major cell type that is responsible for protection against Pseudomonas pneumonia in the setting on chemotherapy-induced neutropenic.
the authors have identified a new population of lung resident macro phages that can be expanded by vaccination, and that are able to provide protective immunity against bacterial pneumonia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a new kind of lung Wbc that survives chemotherapy.
we found a population in the lung that is stable to chemotherapy and can engulf and clear bacteria.

the vaccine-induced macrophage (VIM) population is a chemotherapy-stable, lung-resident population of macrophages that can be expanded and activated by vaccination and that mediates protection against lethal infection during neutropenia.

there is a kind of macrophage in the lung that survives chemotherapy.
a population of lung resident macro phages can be activated to engulf and remove bacteria.
